In performance the three sizes often play the same melody together in one large ensemble, forming three parts at fixed intervals, accompanied by percussion such as the tinya and the wankar. This kind of traditional music is called tarqueada. The instrument is an aerophone flute with a duct at the blowing end and a free hole at the far end, and its timbre is deeper and more penetrating than the recorder's.

Its range is wide, and it speaks effectively from the deep weight of the low register to the clear sharpness of the top. The airstream sets the column of air around the fingerholes vibrating, which gives an unusual harmonic structure. The middle and low register is warm and full, close to the warmth of clay flutes; the top is crisp and bright, comparable to the bamboo flute. Against the recorder its timbre has more folk character and a rawer texture; against the transverse flute it sounds fuller and stronger. The overall sound is both lyrical and expressive and can carry complex melodic lines, which gives it an important place in South American folk music.

The tarka (tarka; tharqa in Quechua and Aymara) is an aerophone of the Andean peoples, of the vertical-flute kind, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.221.12. The body is usually wooden, with six fingerholes, a duct at the blowing end and a free hole at the far end. It is shorter than the recorder and more angular in outline, needs more air to play, and its timbre is darker and penetrating. It comes in three sizes, large, medium and small, the middle a fifth above the low and the high an octave above it; the three often play the melody together in a large ensemble, divided into parts at fixed intervals, accompanied by percussion such as the tinya and wankar, and the traditional genre is called tarqueada.
